nodes.name: Precipitation synthesis of MNF
nodes.procedure: First, the metal source (nickel acetate tetrahydrate and ferrous chloride; 0.5 mmol) was dissolved in ethanol (200 ml) and heated to 90 °C, then ammonia (2 ml) was added dropwise to the solution with vigorous stirring. After that, deionized water (100 ml) was added into the mixture. This mixture was then held at 90 °C for 1.5 h under vigorous stirring. After cooling to room temperature, the product was collected through vacuum filtration and re-dispersed into water. After being sonicated for 30 min, the mixture was filtered again through vacuum filtration. The sonication and cleaning steps were repeated at least three times, and the product was collected and dispersed in deionized water (30 ml) for further use.

nodes.name: MNF ink preparation
nodes.procedure: First, the catalyst (~35 mg) was dispersed in deionized water (30 ml) and sonicated in solution to give a clear yellowish ink. Then, this yellowish ink (0.5 ml) was mixed with methanol (0.5 ml). The mixture was sonicated for 30 min to yield a homogeneously dispersed catalyst ink.

nodes.name: MNF electrode on carbon paper
nodes.procedure: Then, the catalyst ink (20 μl) was drop cast onto carbon paper (0.5 × 0.4 cm; Toray Carbon Paper 090, Fuel Cell Store) and dried in air. Subsequently, the electrode was dried further using a vacuum oven at 120 °C for 6 h. The mass loading of the catalysts was around 0.06 mg cm⁻², as calculated from the concentration and volume of the catalyst ink cast onto the carbon paper.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance shows reversible mass changes during cyclic voltammetry scans between 1.13 and 1.63 V vs RHE, with mass increase at more positive potentials linked to OER current density.
nodes.evidence_snippet: There is a clear link between the OER current density and mass change (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Notably, reversible mass changes are observed during cyclic voltammetry scans (Fig. 1a), with an increase in electrode mass at more positive potentials.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando synchrotron X-ray fluorescence microscopy reveals Ni and Fe species distribution from electrode to electrolyte with ~10 μm interfacial diffusion layer, showing positive correlation between fluorescence intensity (metal concentration) and OER current density.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A boundary differentiating the electrode and electrolyte becomes apparent in the Ni distribution map, delineating an interfacial diffusion layer that spans around 10 μm into the electrolyte (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9).

nodes.characterization_summary: UV-vis spectroscopy detects FeO₄²⁻ species formation after chronoamperometry at 1.73 V vs RHE, showing characteristic double peaks at 505 and 582 nm with concentrations of 1.99 and 1.75 μmol l⁻¹ respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Clear double peaks at around 505 and 582 nm appeared after long-term chronoamperometry measurements at both potentials, which is an indication that the FeO₄²⁻ species have been formed during the OER.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy shows pronounced pre-edge peak at 7,114.9 eV indicative of FeO₄²⁻; EXAFS reveals Fe–O peak at ~1.05 Å (fitted bond length 1.65 Å) matching FeO₄²⁻ reference, confirming FeO₄²⁻ species presence during OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The spectra of the K₂FeO₄ solution and the solid K₂FeO₄ pellet feature two key characteristics: a pronounced pre-edge peak at around 7,114.9 eV and a reduced white line intensity, both of which are indicative of FeO₄²⁻. The peak at ~1.05 Å is also evident for our MNF sample when measured at 1.63 V vs RHE (Fig. 2d), which is clear evidence that FeO₄²⁻ species were present during the OER.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando hard X-ray absorption spectroscopy at Fe and Ni K-edges reveals dynamic electronic behavior of Fe species during OER, with Fe oxidation state oscillations at OER onset (1.43 V vs RHE) and pronounced dynamic structural alterations beyond second scattering shell at 1.53 V vs RHE.
nodes.evidence_snippet: A noteworthy observation is the oscillation in the oxidation state of Fe at the OER onset potential (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). Relative to the Ni centre, the Fe local structure demonstrates more pronounced dynamic alterations at OER potentials, especially beyond the second scattering shell.

nodes.characterization_summary: Surface-sensitive O K-edge XAS identifies O 2p holes (μ_O⁻ at 528.5 eV, μ₂-O at 529 eV) on MNF catalyst surface after OER, with decreased intensity at 1.63 V vs RHE indicating O-O bond formation promotion by mobile Fe species.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Obvious O 2p holes are identified using O K-edge XAS (indicated by the broad pre-edge peak in the range of 527–530 eV) after the OER, which correspond to 2p electron-deficient oxygen sites μ_O⁻ at 528.5 eV and μ₂-O at 529 eV on the catalyst surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando HERFD-XAS at MNF electrode interface (8 μm from surface) shows enhanced pre-edge peak intensity at 7,114 eV indicating higher oxidation state of mobile Fe species (>3+) under OER conditions.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Under the OER conditions, the normalized intensity of the pre-edge peak for the MNF interface is higher than that of Fe³⁺ in the bulk electrolyte at the OCP, which confirms that the average oxidation state of the mobile Fe species near the MNF electrode under the OER conditions is higher than 3+.
